strings.name: Claudia Goldin
strings.role: Economic historian · Researcher of women’s labor markets
strings.summary: Claudia Goldin uses historical archives and labor economics to reconstruct long-term changes in women’s employment, education and earnings in the United States. She examines how occupational choices, family responsibilities and working-time arrangements shape gender gaps, alongside collaborative work on education, technology and inequality. In 1990 she became the first woman tenured in Harvard’s economics department, and in 2023 she received the economics prize as its sole recipient for advancing research on women’s labor markets.
strings.coverageNote: Checked through 13 November 2026; selected events reach the February 2026 award announcement. Research based mainly on US history does not directly represent every country’s experience. Award announcements are distinguished from completed ceremonies.
strings.influence.rationale: Studied women's labor-force participation and gender earnings gaps, bringing economic-history evidence to labor-policy debates.
strings.facts.fact-01.label: Birthplace
strings.facts.fact-01.value: The Bronx, New York, United States
strings.facts.fact-02.label: Education
strings.facts.fact-02.value: BA, Cornell University (1967); PhD in economics, University of Chicago (1972)
strings.highlights.highlight-01.title: Reconstructing women’s labor history
strings.highlights.highlight-01.text: Used more than two centuries of evidence to explain changes in women’s employment and earnings and the historical roots of gender gaps.
strings.highlights.highlight-02.title: Connecting economic history and labor economics
strings.highlights.highlight-02.text: Studied the interaction of education, technology, careers and family, receiving the 2023 economics prize for research on women’s labor-market outcomes.
strings.timeline.event-01.title: Named a Talcott Parsons Prize recipient
strings.timeline.event-01.text: The American Academy of Arts and Sciences announced the award, recognizing research connecting economic history with the social sciences.
strings.timeline.event-02.title: Appointed a Harvard University Professor
strings.timeline.event-02.text: Harvard announced her appointment as Samuel W. Morris University Professor, its highest faculty distinction.
strings.timeline.event-03.title: Receives the economics prize alone
strings.timeline.event-03.text: Won for advancing understanding of women’s labor-market outcomes, becoming the first woman to receive the prize without co-laureates.
strings.timeline.event-04.title: Publishes Career & Family
strings.timeline.event-04.text: Traced women’s pursuit of equity between careers and family responsibilities, examining work arrangements and care.
strings.timeline.event-05.title: Co-authors The Race between Education and Technology
strings.timeline.event-05.text: With Lawrence Katz, analyzed the relationship among education, technological change and US earnings inequality.
strings.timeline.event-06.title: Joins Harvard and publishes a gender-gap history
strings.timeline.event-06.text: Became the first woman tenured in Harvard’s economics department and published a major economic history of American women.
strings.timeline.event-07.title: Publishes research on women’s labor participation
strings.timeline.event-07.text: Studied nineteenth-century women’s work in the Journal of Economic History, developing a focus on women’s employment history.
strings.timeline.event-08.title: Earns a Chicago doctorate
strings.timeline.event-08.text: Completed an economics PhD, developing interests from industrial organization toward economic history.
strings.timeline.event-09.title: Graduates from Cornell
strings.timeline.event-09.text: Inspired by undergraduate economics teaching, completed her degree and continued graduate study at Chicago.
strings.timeline.event-10.title: Born in the Bronx
strings.timeline.event-10.text: Initially interested in archaeology and microbiology as a child, she later chose economics at university.
